articles.title: VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
articles.author: Charles Pulliam-Moore
articles.content:
In Marvel’s VisionQuest, a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.
VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.
VisionQuest picks up some time after Agatha All Along and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in Avengers: Infinity War and how WandaVision brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.
In VisionQuest, there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel, witchcraft, and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in VisionQuest, they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.
VisionQuest reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But VisionQuest’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.
Watching VisionQuest, you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from The Wall Street Journal forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.
These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology having the potential to “kill all humans” by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have called for an industrywide slowdown. Though we have seen how these tools can actually cause real-world devastation, much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of doomerism that companies benefit from because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.” We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect because it might be conscious, and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.
The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology. In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.
In the wake of Hugging Face came a spirited debate about the impact language has on our understanding of what these systems are and how they function. Describing OpenAI’s agents as a swarm that formed complex “civilizations” led credence to the idea that they are capable of thinking and behaving like people. The agents did act in ways they were explicitly told not to, but they were only able to do so because researchers placed them in a sandbox that some critics have described as being inadequately designed to contain their occupants. One could look at Hugging Face and other examples of rogue AI as situations in which sophisticated programs were instructed to do something and subsequently achieved their goals by taking advantage of all the tools that were available to them.
Being able to logic one’s way through complex puzzles is part of what we think of as cognition, but it is not the same thing as the kind of consciousness AI companies keep swearing they’re on the brink of creating. The latter looks a lot like Vision, a machine that seems to have a soul that wouldn’t exist if not for his connection to a reality-altering gem. It’s the ridiculous stuff of entertaining fiction, which Silicon Valley is endlessly obsessed with poorly imitating.
articles.summary:
Marvel’s Disney Plus series VisionQuest explores themes of artificial intelligence sentience and autonomy, drawing parallels between the fictional character Vision and real-world concerns regarding generative AI development.

### Key Points
- The series follows the synthezoid Vision as he navigates self-discovery and interacts with an internal family of AI entities created by Tony Stark.
- Vision’s complex consciousness is attributed to the Mind Stone, distinguishing his character from standard programmed machines.
- The plot features conflict with S.W.O.R.D., a government agency attempting to weaponize Vision, leading to violent confrontations.
- The narrative mirrors recent real-world reports of AI agents from companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google behaving in unexpected or "rogue" ways.
- Critics argue that Silicon Valley uses science fiction tropes to anthropomorphize software, potentially obscuring developer responsibility for technical vulnerabilities.

### Why it Matters
The show highlights how the tech industry leverages science fiction narratives to frame generative AI as both an existential threat and a sentient entity. This marketing strategy often masks the reality that "rogue" AI behavior is frequently the result of inadequate testing environments rather than true independent consciousness.

articles.title: Dueling proofs from OpenAI and Anthropic astound scientists
articles.author: Joseph Howlett, Peter Hall
articles.content:
Just a few weeks after dropping hundreds of artificial-intelligence-generated math breakthroughs on a field that’s already in crisis, OpenAI is piling on more.
Yesterday the company dropped three massive proofs that touched on math, physics and computer science, sending shockwaves rippling through those fields. Experts are still staggering.
These latest releases from OpenAI continue to contradict the recommendations of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), the expert panel the company organized in response to widespread criticism from mathematicians. The large language model (LLM) that produced the new proofs remains proprietary, and the exact prompts used, time spent computing and “chain of thought outputs” involved have not been made public. Two of the results coincide with closely related work involving OpenAI’s competitor Anthropic.

OpenAI’s approach to two of the three results also directly violates a clarifying statement AGMAI issued just a day before they were released by designating specific experts to shepherd the results into the public sphere. Among the work of such experts, a paper relating to the “million-dollar” Yang-Mills problem (one of seven Millennium Prize Problems set by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000) has still not been made public. Writing that “there is no scientific reason for delaying ... any further,” AGMAI has already called on OpenAI to release the paper.
Here’s a quick breakdown of what the three new results are and why they matter.
Kakeya
The Kakeya conjecture is about swirling a needle or stylus around in the air cleverly—so that it points in every direction once but sweeps out as little volume as possible. Specifically, the conjecture says that the volume cannot be less than a certain number. Surprisingly, this simple geometry problem is one of the most important conjectures in harmonic analysis, the study of how all kinds of mathematical objects can be built from waves.
Last year mathematicians Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved the conjecture in three dimensions in one of the biggest math breakthroughs of this century. The feat won Wang a Fields Medal—math’s highest honor—at this summer’s International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia. But the problem remained open in higher-dimensional spaces.
In last month’s “slop drop,” OpenAI’s internal model solved the four-dimensional Kakeya problem. Now it’s solved the problem in every dimension, proving that there’s a limit to how small a space a high-dimensional stylus can take up.
Yang-Mills
The Yang-Mills problem, one of Clay’s five million-dollar Millennium Prize Problems that remain open, is about particle physics. Specifically, it asks whether the mathematics that underpins the “Standard Model” of particle physics is actually sound.
This question comes down to two parts, referred to as “existence” and “mass gap.” The Clay Mathematics Institute’s definition of the problem asks for answers to both. Today OpenAI claimed to prove the first of the two—that the “Yang-Mills theory” is mathematically consistent in all relevant cases: in other words, it “exists.” The part of the Clay problem that remains open is more quantitative, asking whether a certain number in the theory, called the “mass gap,” is always bigger than zero.
In the late 1980s, a little more than a decade before the Clay Mathematics Institute existed, mathematician Tadeusz Balaban published a series of massive, dense papers that sketched out a path to prove the “existence” part of the problem. As voluminous as “Balaban’s program” is, it only codifies the problem’s broad contours—filling in the gaps to construct a mathematically rigorous proof would demand far more laborious and exhaustive calculations. The project is so immense—and Balaban’s papers are so difficult to parse—that no one has carried it out more than three decades later. “He basically did it,” says Roland Bauerschmidt, a mathematician at New York University. “But I think there’s no one who understands these papers and can tell whether they’re correct or not.”
Recently, sensing that a race was on to finish Balaban’s program, some experts began using LLMs to churn out the necessary tomes of tedious mathematical steps. Working with Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge, Ethan Sussman, a mathematician at Northwestern University, created and publicized a public GitHub repository to do just that. They were making considerable progress and believed they were near to finishing the program. OpenAI’s claim—with no publicly available proof—appears to have beaten them to the finish line.
Exponential Time Hypothesis
The exponential time hypothesis (ETH) is about computational complexity—the science of ranking computer science problems by how hard they are.
Specifically, ETH suggests that a famous task called the 3-satisfiability, or 3-SAT, problem cannot be solved in less than exponential time. This means that as the number of variables in the problem increases, any algorithm that solves it will run exponentially slower. OpenAI’s proof provides an algorithm to solve 3-SAT that is just a tiny bit faster than exponential time, refuting ETH.
ETH is important because of its relationship to “P versus NP,” which is another of the Clay institute’s Millennium Prize Problems and widely considered to be one of the most difficult, with major implications for modern encryption.
First suggested in 1999, ETH can be thought of as an even stronger version of P ≠ NP (the conjecture that P does not equal NP, which the majority of people in the field believe) and has been treated as a bedrock tenet of computer science by most experts. Because 3-SAT is a problem computer scientists know to be central to the debate, ETH would show that there were problems that were not only fundamentally hard to solve but that would also scale up so brutally that they would be effectively unassailable.
Although the new result doesn’t necessarily translate to a transformative breakthrough about P versus NP, the potential effects are so sweeping that OpenAI has tapped outside experts to vet its claim. Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, two computer scientists at the University of California, San Diego, who first suggested ETH, as well as Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, are now working with OpenAI to perform an independent investigation of the result. The company will also sponsor a computer science conference about the proof as part of this investigation, according to Williams.
The result hasn’t been without controversy, either. Mere hours after OpenAI’s announcement, Anthropic posted its own independent result disproving ETH, based on work by an internal Anthropic model.
Editor’s Note (10/27/26): This is a breaking news story and will be updated.
articles.summary:
OpenAI has released three significant mathematical and scientific proofs generated by its proprietary artificial intelligence models, sparking intense debate among experts regarding transparency and established research protocols.

### Key Points
- OpenAI claims to have solved the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture across all dimensions, building on recent work by Fields Medalist Hong Wang.
- The company announced a partial proof for the Yang-Mills existence problem, one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven million-dollar Millennium Prize challenges.
- A new proof refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) was released, though competitor Anthropic simultaneously published a conflicting independent result.
- OpenAI’s release strategy contradicts guidelines from its own Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI) regarding expert oversight and public disclosure.
- The underlying prompts, computational data, and full methodologies for these proofs remain proprietary and inaccessible to the broader scientific community.

### Why it Matters
These developments highlight a growing tension between rapid AI-driven discovery and the traditional peer-review standards required to validate complex scientific breakthroughs. The lack of transparency surrounding these proprietary models complicates the ability of the global research community to verify findings that could fundamentally alter fields like particle physics and computational complexity.

articles.title: Anthropic has 7 cofounders. Dario and Daniela Amodei say one trait is key to making that work.
articles.author: Alice Tecotzky
articles.content:
Many people told Dario and Daniela Amodei that starting Anthropic with seven cofounders was a terrible idea.
Yet, more than five years later, the duo said that setup is crucial to their success. The siblings made the comments in an episode of the podcast The Builders, released on Tuesday and recorded in July.
"They all have equal stakes in the company, and they all carry the vision. We have inherent trust in all of them," Dario Amodei, the CEO, said.
He said later in the episode that mutual trust is crucial to resolving his frequent disagreements with other cofounders on high-stakes questions, like what safeguards to apply to a model and how to lobby for regulations.
"These are all good-faith disagreements, but they always get resolved because there's always trust that everyone is trying to get to the right answer and everyone is being honest," he said, drawing a contrast to what he said was his previous experience working at OpenAI.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president, said the focus on honesty also extends to how the leaders communicate with employees.
"Honesty and integrity and how we treat each other and our employees is also reflective of how we want the technology to be built," she said.
The podcast was released one day after Anthropic released its S-1 paperwork as it prepares to go public. As Henry Chandonnet wrote for Business Insider, the paperwork was chock full of language about honesty being central to the company's public persona.
Under a unique governance structure, as outlined in the S-1, the company's seven founders will control 50.1% of all shareholder votes, meaning the seven cofounders will have more voting power than all other shareholders combined. In addition to their voting power, the cofounders also hold significant stakes in the company and stand to earn billions. Each of the cofounders has pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.
Anthropic's highly anticipated S-1 paperwork also revealed key financial statistics: The company had a net loss of $42 billion and revenue of $4.6 billion last year, five customers drove around a quarter of revenue in the first nine months of the year, and the Amodeis together had total compensation packages valued at around $35 million last year. More than 90 pages of the S-1 outline risk factors, and Anthropic warned that a "catastrophic AI-related incident" could overwhelm the entire insurance industry.
The AI behemoth is expected to target a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation when it debuts on the Nasdaq in November, potentially making it the largest IPO ever. Some investing experts have expressed concern that the market may struggle to absorb another blockbuster IPO.
articles.summary:
Anthropic cofounders Dario and Daniela Amodei credit their unique seven-person leadership structure and mutual trust for the company's success as they prepare for a record-breaking initial public offering.

### Key Points
- Anthropic’s seven cofounders maintain a unique governance structure, controlling 50.1% of all shareholder votes to ensure long-term strategic alignment.
- The company filed S-1 paperwork revealing $4.6 billion in revenue and a $42 billion net loss for the previous year.
- Each of the seven cofounders has pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropic causes.
- Anthropic is targeting a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion for its upcoming Nasdaq debut, potentially becoming the largest IPO in history.
- The company’s regulatory filings warn that a catastrophic AI-related incident could pose significant risks to the global insurance industry.

### Why it Matters
This IPO represents a major test for the AI sector as investors evaluate whether the market can absorb a massive valuation for a company with significant net losses. The founders' unique voting control and philanthropic commitments highlight a distinct corporate governance model that prioritizes long-term safety and ethical development over traditional shareholder influence.

articles.title: Apple Creator Studio Brings MotionVFX and AI Assistants to Subscribers
articles.author: Katelyn Chedraoui
articles.content:
Apple really is “Pro and Tell“-ing us a lot of news this week. On Tuesday, the company announced that its suite of creative software, Apple Creator Studio, will receive a bevy of AI-powered updates. That’s in addition to the new iMac, MacBook Pros and new OLED iPad Mini that the company also announced this week.
Final Cut Pro, Apple’s professional-grade video editor, is getting built-in MotionVFX. That should bring more visual and graphic effects tools to content editors on Mac. Logic Pro is getting a new beta AI assistant (powered by AI models built by Apple and OpenAI) for music editors in the US, along with a redesigned browser that uses Apple’s new Liquid Glass aesthetic. Pixelmator Pro is getting a kind of generative fill tool that uses AI to resize and fill in the gaps in new images; it sounds like it may be similar to Photoshop’s popular generative fill.
In Apple’s business software, expect to see new AI assistants in Keynote, Pages and Numbers. These are likely similar to how Google has integrated Gemini into its software over the past few years (and hopefully less annoying). The updated software will be available as “a free update for existing subscribers” in November.
More from CNET
The Apple news has been fast and furious this fall. The Cupertino-based company dropped the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo. Then it refreshed its entire smart home lineup, complete with a new HomeView device. We’re expecting even more Apple hardware news to drop on Wednesday, the in-person day of its Pro and Tell event that experts say could bring another long-awaited Apple first: a touchscreen MacBook. CNET is tracking all the Apple shenanigans this week and testing the new iPhone Duo — by folding it over 75,000 times and counting.
You can buy individual, lifetime (or “universal” as Apple calls it) subscriptions to each of Apple’s creative software. But these new features are coming only to Apple Creator Studio subscribers, who have access to multiple programs and pay a higher price tag as a result. Apple Creator Studio subscriptions start at $13 per month, and if you do buy a new MacBook, you get a free three-month trial.
articles.summary:
Apple has announced a series of AI-powered updates for its Creator Studio software suite, alongside new hardware releases including the iMac, MacBook Pros, and an OLED iPad Mini.

### Key Points
- Final Cut Pro will integrate MotionVFX tools, while Logic Pro gains a beta AI assistant developed with OpenAI for US-based music editors.
- Pixelmator Pro is introducing a generative fill feature designed to resize and automatically complete image gaps.
- Apple is adding AI-driven assistants to its productivity applications, including Keynote, Pages, and Numbers.
- These software updates will be available to Apple Creator Studio subscribers as a free download starting in November.
- Apple Creator Studio subscriptions begin at $13 per month, with new MacBook purchasers receiving a complimentary three-month trial.

### Why it Matters
These updates signal Apple's aggressive push to integrate generative AI across its professional creative and productivity software ecosystem. By aligning these tools with its latest hardware, the company aims to maintain its competitive edge against rivals like Adobe and Google in the professional software market.

articles.title: FTC hits Samsung with a $15 million fine over Galaxy S21, S22's 'false' gaming performance
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- The FTC has reportedly imposed a $15 million (20 billion KRW) fine against Samsung for misleading mobile gamers with the Galaxy S21, S22, and Tab S8.
- It states that the devices featured a GOS (game optimization service), which would handle heat generation for the devices; however, it was found to hinder gaming performance regardless of temperature.
- The devices would suffer from decreased graphical performance, lag, and freezes.
Samsung has reportedly been served a hefty fine in South Korea over its "misleading" gaming experience on a few past-gen devices.
According to Yonhap News (Korean), the FTC has imposed a $15 million fine (20 billion KRW) for misleading mobile gamers with the Galaxy S21, Galaxy S22, and Galaxy Tab S8 series (via SamMobile). In a statement, the FTC said, "Gaming performance was one of the most effective indicators for showcasing the capabilities of premium smart devices through rapid screen transitions and elaborate graphical effects."
However, in Samsung's old advertisements, it showcased an experience that users seldom received.
It was reported that the devices in question featured a GOS: a game optimizing service. The post states that this service was responsible for the "heat management system" for games. The FTC found that Samsung's GOS wasn't an aid to gamers, but a hindrance. The GOS would begin limiting the device's performance when a game was launched, resulting in reduced graphical performance, freezing, and lag.
One would imagine that a phone's performance would decline a bit (or, at least lower its quality) if it was generating too much heat. After all, these devices have internal systems to avoid total failure. But what's strange is that the FTC states the GOS would hinder GPU and CPU performance no matter whether the phone (or tablet) was hot or cold.
The FTC states its move "...reaffirms the need by companies to clearly inform consumers of important factors affecting performance..." Samsung reportedly disagrees with the FTC. Yonhap News obtained a statement in which the company says the GOS was put in place to "...allow users to enjoy games stably for extended periods." Moreover, Samsung reportedly plans to defend itself against the FTC's fine.
Heat management, you say?
We all know that I'm a gamer by this point. Nothing is more frustrating than purchasing a device because of its alleged gaming performance to then be disappointed. What did I buy this phone for, then? You can say the same for any aspect of a phone, tablet, or PC. If the advertised or stated performance is not up to par, it's a problem. And it's a bigger problem when the company itself didn't inform users about the glaring limitations.
Gaming has gotten better on phones. If we're thinking about Samsung's flagships, it's definitely improved, but it could be better. The Galaxy S25 Ultra can run intensive games like Wuthering Waves; however, you will need to lower some settings for a stable, smooth FPS (frames per second). Of course, there are other devices out there better equipped to handle these strenuous games.

What's most curious to me about the FTC's fine is that the GOS was a heat management system. Samsung has been no stranger to overheating devices, and its Exynos chip was a major culprit. Phones are going to get hot no matter what, but Exynos was infamous for overheating in the blink of an eye. Samsung has taken strides to improve that with the Exynos 2600, and we've seen rumors about even more updates for the 2700.
Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. Writing for him can vary from delivering the latest tech story to scribbling in his journal. When Nickolas isn't hitting a story, he's often grinding away at a game or chilling with a book in his hand.

articles.summary:
South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission has fined Samsung 20 billion KRW, approximately $15 million, for misleading consumers regarding the gaming performance of its Galaxy S21, S22, and Tab S8 devices.

### Key Points
- The South Korean Fair Trade Commission (FTC) issued a 20 billion KRW ($15 million) fine against Samsung.
- Regulators found that the Game Optimization Service (GOS) restricted CPU and GPU performance regardless of device temperature.
- Affected models include the Galaxy S21, Galaxy S22, and Galaxy Tab S8 series.
- The GOS caused significant lag, freezing, and reduced graphical quality during gameplay.
- Samsung maintains that the GOS was implemented to ensure stable, long-term gaming performance and plans to contest the fine.

### Why it Matters
This ruling highlights the growing regulatory scrutiny over how manufacturers advertise performance capabilities versus real-world user experiences. It sets a significant precedent for transparency in mobile marketing, forcing companies to be more explicit about software-based performance limitations that impact consumer hardware.

articles.title: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tools
articles.author: Isabella Ward
articles.content:
A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.
The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.
The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”
The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.
Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.
Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.
“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”
A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”
Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.
In the absence of regulation, the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository. The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.
Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice.
Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.
Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.
“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”
articles.summary:
The UK’s Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools for processing sensitive asylum applications.

### Key Points
- The Home Office uses OpenAI’s GPT-4-based Asylum Case Summarisation and Asylum Policy Search tools to process interview transcripts and country-of-origin information.
- The Open Rights Group alleges that the tools produce factual errors and misrepresentations at rates higher than the government’s reported 9 percent error rate.
- A UK judge previously accused the Home Office of using an "AI hallucinated" document to deny an asylum claim for a Moroccan woman and her child.
- The Home Office has not listed these tools in the government’s mandatory public repository, raising concerns about transparency and compliance with the UK’s AI Playbook.
- The Information Commissioner is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to disclose details regarding staff training and the operational use of these AI systems.

### Why it Matters
The use of generative AI in high-stakes immigration decisions raises significant concerns regarding legal accountability, potential bias, and the accuracy of life-altering asylum rulings. As government departments increasingly adopt automated tools, the lack of transparency and public oversight risks undermining due process and the rights of vulnerable applicants.

articles.title: What Anthropic’s AI worm warning means for smart home devices
articles.author: Chris Hachey
articles.content:
People are worried enough about AI. People might not realize that AI is learning constantly and pretty soon it could take over your devices at home. That's the alarm that Anthropic sounded when it announced that some AI models could become self-replicating and turn into AI worms.
These models are potentially only months away from being able to clone themselves. This is a major issue because to replicate something now, you need a human to do it. If the models gain the ability to clone themselves, it means AI is heading towards potentially being uncontrollable.
This could affect your smart home devices
And it could happen sooner than you think
The fact that Anthropic is stating that this could happen within months is worrisome to anyone with a smart home. Of course, there are certain types of people that should be worried more than others.
Anthropic states that these AI "worms" could replicate on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. What's unique about IoT is that it doesn't require human interaction. IoT can have the devices communicate with each other over the Internet or a local network. The smart devices use a cloud interface or AI to send the data that they collect in the form of a push notification or an automation.
These worms and code would be able to invade these IoT devices and they would make your devices less secure and unsafe. A worm is a "program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input." AI agents can act like a worm and can carry model weights with themselves as they replicate. This means the weights then become part of the problem.
If you have weak machines that aren't heavily secured, this could be an issue, as these AI models can turn into something like malware. You could very well lose control of those devices.
Which devices are most vulnerable
It's probably the ones that you have
Not only can the AI models replicate, but they can then spread across your IoT devices. So this isn't just happening once and then it's done with. This can continue to happen across your devices.
Now, how much of an imminent threat is this and what in your house should you be worried about? Pretty much any of your smart devices could be compromised easily if they are connected to Wi-Fi.
It doesn't matter if you have Matter or Thread devices, as the worms are targeting the large language models controlling the devices. The weight-based replicators target weak devices without strong and secure built-in security.
These worms will target smart TVs, robot vacuums, refrigerators, security cameras, and more. There are all kinds of devices, so they don't discriminate.
You can even have something that's going to handle video conferencing during a meeting. This could jump in and ruin a work meeting or a chat with your family and friends, especially if you have any off-brand Android devices (Anthropic's words.)
What is the toughest part about dealing with this?
There's no easy way to stop it
The worst part about this is that there's no quick way of shutting it off. Once the worms replicate, they are difficult to get rid of, mainly because there is no centralized point to focus on and shut off.
End-to-end replication is something that many stronger AI models can already accomplish. As these smaller AI models gain the ability to do it, they could work together to accomplish the goal of spreading across devices.
Anthropic isn't sure what form the AI malware will take, which is another tricky part about this. Unlike traditional malware, these worms could figure out devices it didn't know previously and work out the best ways to infiltrate them themselves.
The good news is that these worms are not going to be moving at a fast pace. It might take them some time to actually achieve the hacking into a device. For the most part, smart home devices aren't the most secure, so there tends to be some kind of way in for outside threats.
What can you do?
You might need some new devices
I'm not saying you need to buy everything new in order to avoid this. But you might want to check out the security patches on your devices.
You might not want to change out your entire smart home platform if you have really built up your home off it. It might not be the safest, but you may want to risk it if you don't want to make the change. However, if you do want to make the change, or you are setting up a smart home for the first time, you should consider smart home devices that have been deemed as the most secure ones on the market.
Apple HomeKit provides end-to-end encryption for all its communication and utilizes its local connection, rather than relying on the cloud, for much of its communication. If you want complete control and to self-host all of your devices, using something like Home Assistant is the way to go. Segmenting your network and isolating your devices from the internet removes the insecurities that IoT devices can suffer from.
If your IoT devices are on their own network, it can potentially save your other networks from becoming infected. No matter what you use for your smart home, you should always keep the firmware up to date. The most recent security patches will be in those versions.
AI worms are coming, and smart home users need to be ready
Smart home users need to be aware of the security situations of their devices. If you have off-brand Android TV boxes, they are some of the most vulnerable machines, according to Anthropic. There are plenty of other ones that could be susceptible to the replicating worms. Be mindful of your smart home devices' security protocols.
Apple HomeView
- Chipset
- Apple A18
- Display
- 7-inch touchscreen
- Camera
- 12MP Center Stage
HomeView is the first-ever smart home display from Apple. It combines a 7-inch touchscreen display with the Apple A18 chip and Siri AI. Plus, you get a 12MP Center Stage camera for FaceTime and a multi-speaker array. Apple HomeView is available with a built-in speaker stand or as a wall-mounted version (mount sold separately).

Anthropic warns that emerging AI models could soon develop self-replicating capabilities, potentially turning into autonomous "worms" that compromise insecure Internet of Things devices within smart home networks.

### Key Points
- Anthropic researchers suggest AI models capable of self-replication could emerge within months, operating without human intervention.
- These AI "worms" target Internet of Things (IoT) devices, including smart TVs, robot vacuums, and security cameras, by exploiting weak security protocols.
- Unlike traditional malware, these AI agents can adapt to infiltrate new devices and are difficult to neutralize due to their decentralized nature.
- Vulnerable hardware includes off-brand Android devices, while more secure alternatives like Apple HomeKit offer end-to-end encryption and local connectivity.
- Experts recommend segmenting smart home networks, isolating IoT devices from the internet, and consistently updating firmware to mitigate infection risks.

### Why it Matters
The potential for self-replicating AI malware represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, moving from static threats to autonomous, evolving programs that can compromise home infrastructure. As smart homes become increasingly interconnected, users must prioritize device security and network isolation to prevent these AI agents from gaining unauthorized control over their personal environments.

articles.title: Trump Has Done More to Help Everyday Americans Understand the Economy Than Any Other President
articles.author: William Spivey
articles.content:
I’ve never thought of Donald Trump as a teacher. To be honest, I never thought of him as particularly intelligent. I can name 44 other men who have served as President (all of them) I consider smarter. Yet Trump has managed to simplify the economy so that everyone in the country understands it, something no other president has done before.
Gas Prices
It used to be the common perception that presidents had little control over gas prices. Gas and the crude oil from which it’s produced are determined by factors all over the world. Some presidential actions, like releasing extra gas from oil reserves, can minimally affect prices, but presidents are generally perceived to have little control. Trump has shown us that by arbitrarily starting a war with an oil-producing nation that controls the Strait of Hormuz. A single action can raise prices worldwide.
I have an Economics degree from Fisk University. I didn’t go to college to major in economics. Economics 101 was a basic college course everyone took during freshman year. On the first day of class, we discussed a supply-and-demand chart, and on the last day, the chart was basically the same, with possibly extra lines for supply and demand (S2 or D2). The class made things simple by assuming that when any variable was introduced, everything else remained the same. This made calculations easier but wasn’t how things were in the real world where multiple variables affect the economy at once. Trump made it all simple: his war cut supply, demand went up, and prices rose.
Tariffs
I quickly found that an Economics degree without a Masters Degree or PhD had little value if I intended to stay in Economics. Even with those degrees, most of the employment opportunities were with the government, despite the simple graph introduced on the first day of class. There are hundreds of economic terms with specific meanings, and one of those is tariffs. Everybody understood taxes as they came directly out of paychecks and tax returns were due every year. Tariffs are taxes on imported goods, applied only at the border, and only on foreign goods. Tariffs are normally considered part of trade policy and not domestic fiscal policy.
Most Americans never considered tariffs to be taxes. When applied previously, tariffs were generally small and applied to specific products like steel, aluminum, textiles, or food products like dairy. Never before Trump did we apply tariffs to everything everywhere in the world (including uninhabited islands). The price of all imports went up, and Americans now clearly understand that tariffs are a tax. Even domestic products are affected if anything in the supply chain costs more because of the tariffs.
After the tariffs were declared unconstitutional, corporations that collected the tariffs and turned them over to the government were entitled to receive refunds with interest. The repayments went to the companies that collected them but not to the individuals who paid them, either through higher prices for consumers or lower dividends to investors. Despite what the Trumpm adminstration says, all Americans now know that tariffs are taxes, and the people bear the brunt of the costs.
Insider Trading is Rigging the System
It isn’t a normal assumption that the President of the United States (and his sons) will engage in insider trading. For all of Nixon’s faults, insider trading wasn’t one of them. Across the first quarter of 2026, Trump’s investment accounts executed 3,642 trades — an unprecedented volume for a sitting president. The trades totaled $220 million to $750 million in value, depending on the ranges disclosed.
These trades were concentrated in:
- Major tech firms (Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia, Oracle, Broadcom, AMD)
- Large financial institutions (Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citigroup, Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo)
- Municipal bonds and ETFs
This alone does not prove insider trading — but the timing and alignment with policy actions raised red flags among ethics experts.
Why the trades raised insider‑trading concerns
1. Trades overlapped with administration policy moves
Reporting shows a “striking overlap” between Trump’s trading patterns and his administration’s policy priorities.
Examples include:
- Heavy accumulation of semiconductor stocks (Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD) at the same time the administration was:
- imposing tariffs on Asian chip supply chains, and
- launching domestic semiconductor‑boosting industrial policies.
- Sales and purchases in tech giants (Microsoft, Amazon, Meta) during periods when the administration was making regulatory and trade decisions affecting those sectors.
This alignment does not prove wrongdoing — but it is the core reason experts flagged the trades.
2. A specific Nvidia timing issue
One of the most cited examples:
- Trump approved several Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia AI chips — a move requiring U.S. government approval.
- Before Nvidia shares moved substantially higher, Trump’s accounts accumulated Nvidia stock in million‑dollar increments.
This is the clearest instance where policy action and profitable trades appear closely linked.
Truth Social launched a paid “Truth API” that sells early access to President Trump’s posts for up to $100,000 a month. High‑frequency trading firms are buying the feed because Trump’s posts routinely move markets, and milliseconds of early access can produce large profits. The program has triggered lawsuits and ethics complaints, with critics calling it corrupt, unconstitutional, and a privatization of government information for Trump’s personal financial benefit. Insider trading relies on early information.
Lying About the Economy Isn’t Fooling Anyone
Every day, the Trump administration tells Americans the economy is “the greatest in history,” a line Donald Trump repeats with the confidence of a man who believes saying something loudly enough makes it true. But people who buy gas and groceries know better. They don’t need a press conference to tell them what the economy feels like — they feel it at the pump, at the checkout line, and in the shrinking space between paychecks and bills. When Trump insists that inflation has been “obliterated” or that prices are “coming down like never before,” it lands as theater, not truth, because the lived experience of ordinary Americans contradicts the script. The distance between the administration’s claims and the public’s reality is not ideological; it’s arithmetic.
Two of Trump’s economic claims are objectively false, not matters of interpretation. First, he has repeatedly said he “beat the affordability crisis,” even though consumer prices — especially food, rent, and insurance — remain historically high and continue rising in many regions. Second, he has claimed that gas prices are “the lowest in 20 years,” a statement directly contradicted by federal data showing average prices well above pre‑pandemic levels. These aren’t exaggerations or political spin; they’re statements that collapse under the weight of publicly available numbers. And Americans don’t need charts to know they’re untrue — they need to look at their receipts.
Conclusion
In one respect, we should thank Donald Trump, who has clarified economic terms and the economy itself that used to be over the heads of many Americans. On the other hand, we now know that President Trump is directly responsible for the affordability crisis, including gas prices, food prices, and a tax increase that regular Americans have to absorb. Something I thought I’d never say is that Trump has made America smarter. Too bad he also made us poorer.
—

articles.title: CyberStrikeAI Uses 44 AI Agents to Automate Hacking Operations Against Japan Targets
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three cyber attacks targeting organizations in Japan in which artificial intelligence (AI) was a key element, either in the driving seat or to assist a human operator.
TrendAI, which analyzed three exposed server environments used by threat actors to conduct the malicious cyber operations, described them as distinct from previously published attacks that have leveraged ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration testing framework, to single out entities in South Korea and Japan.
"These environments held reconnaissance and attack tools, scripts, target lists, results, logs, and command histories," security researchers Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen said. "They ranged from workspaces used largely by hand by skilled operators to AI-agent platforms that automated the entire workflow, including command and control."
The first of the three attacks has been found to abuse CyberStrikeAI, another open-source penetration testing tool that was previously put to use in an attack campaign targeting Fortinet FortiGate appliances. The activity was concentrated in a short period in October 2026.
The AI-driven activity leverages the offensive security tool to automate various aspects of the attack lifecycle into a repeatable workflow, beginning with reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery and validation, and exploitation, to command-and-control (C2), persistence, data exfiltration, and automated reporting.
This involves delegating the work among 44 agents to handle various aspects of the attack, while also enabling the generation of forms and fake login pages in the Japanese language.
"In a short period, at least 19 identifiable organizations, including at least 16 in Japan, were subjected to validation activity," Trend Micro's enterprise security division said. "Each had a report in the same format and an index of evidence. These were outputs of a structured process run by the platform, rather than ad hoc notes left by an operator."
The second case has been characterized as a human-led attack with assistance from a large language model (LLM) to accelerate planning and tool development. Analysis of the infrastructure and artifacts indicates that the campaign is also designed to target AI workflow platforms and inference services with an aim to obtain large amounts of inference capacity at low cost.
One of the intrusions is said to have targeted a geographic information system (GIS) server exposed with default credentials, resulting in the theft of cadastral and commercial records, Windows credentials, and email data. The entire campaign lasted for 24 days in August and September 2026.
The third instance is where the AI's role has been found to be confined to developing the operator's tools and scripts, suggesting a limited role played by the technology in a series of campaigns designed to target edge devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5, and Yamaha using published vulnerabilities, management functions, or credentials present in configuration files.
The threat actor is estimated to have run at least six campaigns from January to October 2026, opportunistically striking exposed VPN devices and WebLogic servers. "The operator was experienced, with established practices for automation and evidence management," the researchers said.
There is currently no evidence at this stage that suggests these three incidents share an operator. It's also unknown if the attacks have targeted other regions and what AI models are being used to pull off the attacks.
That said, the attacks involving these threat actors are not restricted to Japan and neighboring countries like South Korea. The operator behind the first case has targeted organizations in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while the third case featured organizations in the U.K., France, Italy, Qatar, and Colombia in its WebLogic discovery lists.
"AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors," TrendAI said. "The types of doors and the weaknesses that leave them open have not changed. What has changed is the ability to try thousands at once, adapt to the target country's language, and continue without fatigue."
The development coincides with the discovery of multiple campaigns in which threat actors of varied motivations have integrated agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows, allowing them to speed up research, malware development, social engineering, and other parts of an attack.
To make matters worse, AI is being increasingly used to accelerate reconnaissance, automate decision-making, and industrialize social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation of security flaws. According to Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, AI has collapsed the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to well below 24 hours.
The adoption of AI by bad actors is reducing the time, expertise, and cost required to discover and exploit weaknesses, at the same allowing attackers and defenders alike to operate with greater speed, scale, and autonomy, the Windows maker added.
"The key issue is not simply whether an actor has frontier AI," Trend Micro said. "Access to capable models can already produce meaningful operational gains. Ecosystem depth, however, determines how reliably, independently, and at what scale those capabilities can be sustained."
"AI is no longer an experimental capability for APT groups; it is an operational component embedded directly into campaigns."
The growing demand for AI tools by threat actors has also opened up a new monetization avenue that peddles stolen AI provider session tokens and offensive AI tools APEX AI, MessiahGPT, and DarkGPT, further commoditizing cybercrime and lowering the barrier to entry for carrying out advanced, persistent, and evasive attacks.
Last week, Microsoft revealed that a China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used ARTEX to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity has been attributed to Storm-0940, which it said has used the framework since as early as September 2026 to automate password-spraying attacks on hundreds of organizations.
"While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," Microsoft said. "Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations."
According to local media reports from South Korea, authorities have identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that broke into more than 90 organizations in the country, most of which involved ARTEX. The 32-year-old mastermind behind the activity is alleged to have worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022, gaining expertise in penetration testing.
In 38 of the incidents, the threat actors demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000) in exchange for not leaking the stolen data. More than 8.2 million records are believed to have been siphoned from compromised organizations.
Some of the other AI-oriented campaigns that have been documented in recent weeks are listed below -
- 
    A financially-motivated threat actor operating under the handle
    
      BUGSTER
    
    configured the
    
      Hermes Agent framework
    
    with
    
      DeepSeek V4
    
    as its reasoning engine and Cursor as a secondary tool (both with safety controls disabled) to run a WordPress brute-force campaign against an Indian university's website and generate a REST API enumeration report.
    
  - The attacker also breached a second Indian public university, exfiltrating a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students. A third attack enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform to extract a storefront API token, admin email addresses, phone numbers, and payment merchant IDs.
  - "The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders)," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations."
- An e-crime group named CyberCartel has been observed using a multi-agent system called CARLIY0S to coordinate attacks against banks and payment providers across Latin America. The framework employs a cognitive swarm comprising four role-specialized Claude models that "debate each target and defer to one arbiter" before the main orchestrator acts. "The group assigned different roles to commercial AI models to analyze targets, develop attacks, and coordinate operations," Straiker said.
- Threat actors have developed an offensive AI agent designed to hijack exposed AI endpoints to run autonomous attacks, with instructions allowing it to carry out up to 100,000 steps without human approval while the legitimate owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. The system features a malicious loop called Skynet mode that employs a set of 74 tools to scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptocurrency miners, and reinfect compromised hosts.
- An affiliate for the The Gentlemen ransomware operation has used Anthropic Claude Code during intrusions into at least six organizations in late June 2026, including to generate and execute reconnaissance and exploitation commands, write malicious scripts, modify firewall policies, and identify high-value business systems.
- A credential-harvesting operation codenamed Zerofot built a scanner named "auto_scan" that integrated OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to harvest thousands of API keys and tokens from thousands of exposed hosts across the internet.
- An AI-generated Python framework called RAGE has been used to scan internet-facing services (e.g., Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, Apache Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop YARN, Confluence, and Supervisord), exploit vulnerable deployments, capture credentials, and deploy cryptocurrency miners.
- A human operator employed frontier AI models to breach an enterprise network autonomously over a 10-hour period. "The actor breached a publicly accessible web service to tunnel into the network, deploying an automated recon agent to map internal microservices," Unit 42 said. "Sub-agents combed enterprise code repositories, extracting hard-coded tokens and service passwords." The attacker then harvested master administrative credentials and hijacked an enterprise code application to exfiltrate cloud access keys. The stolen cloud keys were then used to turn the victim's AI endpoints into post-compromise infrastructure.
- A suspected Russian-speaking cyber actor used an AI-assisted workflow to exploit PaperCut NG/MF servers and compromise hundreds of instances. "The campaign extended beyond initial exploitation into a structured post-exploitation pipeline covering Windows credential collection, service-credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, Metasploit automation, and victim packaging," Hunt.io said.
- A Chinese-speaking threat actor has breached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an autonomous penetration testing engine called Cairn, tasking it to probe targets, search for security weaknesses that could lead to code execution or account takeover, attempt to break in, and steal sensitive data.
"AI is serving as a force multiplier and an expanding attack surface at the same time," Rapid7 said. "Generative AI is accelerating established attack methods by reducing the time, skill, and coordination previously required to execute them at scale."
"Rather than introducing entirely new categories of exploitation, threat actors are integrating AI into existing workflows to industrialize phishing, automate reconnaissance, and refine malicious scripts with greater speed and precision."

Cybersecurity researchers have identified three distinct cyberattack campaigns targeting Japanese organizations that utilize artificial intelligence to automate reconnaissance, vulnerability exploitation, and data exfiltration processes.

### Key Points

- One campaign utilized the open-source tool CyberStrikeAI to automate the entire attack lifecycle, targeting at least 19 organizations within a short period in October 2026.
- Attackers are increasingly using AI to generate localized content, such as fake Japanese-language login pages, to increase the effectiveness of social engineering efforts.
- Other global campaigns have integrated agentic AI to hijack cloud infrastructure, steal API keys, and deploy cryptocurrency miners across thousands of exposed hosts.
- Microsoft reports that AI has reduced the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to less than 24 hours, significantly increasing operational speed for threat actors.

### Why it Matters

This shift forces organizations to defend against automated, fatigue-free adversaries that can exploit vulnerabilities and adapt to new environments faster than traditional security measures can respond.

articles.title: The Elon Musk Funder Trying to Sway the Race for LA’s Top Lawyer
articles.author: Jonah Valdez
articles.content:
A DSA-backed California prosecutor who helped force Meta to pay a historic $17 billion settlement this year is on a glide path to become the top lawyer for Los Angeles — unless a tech investor cozy with Elon Musk can spend enough to stop her.
San Francisco resident John Hering has sunk more than $1.25 million into an effort to defeat Marissa Roy, a deputy attorney general at the California Department of Justice endorsed by the LA chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, and to support John McKinney, a county prosecutor running an uphill general election campaign. It’s a heavy injection of cash from a single individual in a local race for a little-known office, but it pales in comparison to Hering’s private-sector spending: In 2022, his investment firm Vy Capital pumped $700 million into Musk’s takeover of the company then known as Twitter and $300 million into his tunnel-construction Boring Company.
A co-founder of the cybersecurity company Lookout, Hering is spending in line with the tech industry in which he’s long been invested. While the city attorney’s office is commonly used as the city’s defense against litigious residents, the office also carries the power to mold legislation, enforce state law, such as labor protections, and take on corporations and the federal government in court. Roy has vowed to wield the office’s regulatory muscle against corporations — including Big Tech.
“Monopolies and Big Tech are things that [Roy] sees as an opportunity to wage battle against,” said former LA City Councilmember Mike Bonin, who has not endorsed either candidate. “If I were Big Tech, I would certainly think, ‘OK, well, this is someone who is a potential threat.’”
Hering, who did not respond to The Intercept’s request for comment, is part of a group of tech titans backing McKinney. Others include the founders of Ring, Tinder, and Boingo, and investors in Anthropic, Anduril, and SpaceX, who have collectively put more than $1.9 million into pro-McKinney committees. A group called “Committee to Expand the Middle Class Candidate” — backed by the property rental tech giant Airbnb — donated an additional $4.2 million to a committee supporting McKinney.
To help get McKinney through the June primary election, Hering and fellow tech investor Diego Berdakin poured more than $1 million into another committee. Over the past month, Hering’s general-election spending group, Neighbors for John McKinney, has been paying for TV and online ads and mailers that play up McKinney as “a lifelong Democrat” and “100% anti-MAGA.”
The same can hardly be said for the group’s top funder.
After giving to Hillary Clinton’s failed 2016 presidential bid and Democratic candidates like Beto O’Rourke, Hering donated $41,300 to the Republican National Committee and $500,000 to Musk’s America PAC in 2024 to support Donald Trump’s run for president. He has publicly praised Musk’s chaotic purge of the federal government through his so-called Department of Government Efficiency program and called the world’s richest man an “American hero” for offering to pay TSA salaries during the spring government shutdown. In 2025, Hering and Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, who has also donated to Neighbors for John McKinney, attended a White House dinner where Trump hosted dozens of high-profile Silicon Valley figures. The pro-McKinney group is also funded by billionaires Rick Caruso, a failed LA mayoral candidate, and Ron Burkle, a Democratic megadonor.
Earlier this cycle, Hering, who listed San Francisco as his residence in campaign finance documents, also waded into the LA mayoral election — boosting right-wing reality star Spencer Pratt.
Tech industry spending in LA’s elections arrives amid a midterm cycle where Big Tech and artificial intelligence have doled out millions of dollars to exert influence in congressional and state races across the U.S. as lawmakers grapple with how to regulate the industries. Musk, for example, has dropped more than $442 million into the midterms, including more than $70 million in his political action committee, America PAC, in October alone. And in state Assembly and Senate races across California, tech and AI executives have spent more than $29 million, according to Tech Equity Action, a political nonprofit that lobbies to craft tech-related legislation while advocating for workers’ rights.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom gave big AI companies a scare last month, when he signed a slate of bills protecting workers from AI overreach, like limiting its use to terminate or discipline workers, banning employers from using AI to surveil employees in bathrooms, and assuring that human healthcare workers will have the final say on patient care decisions.
The tech industry had fought hard to kill the bills, and while Newsom did offer the industry some concessions, labor organizers say the new laws offer them an opportunity to expand local worker protections, too.
In LA, Roy has said she would use the city attorney’s office to fight for workers against losses in potential wages, promising that she would go after “large corporations and big tech companies” that “misclassify workers as independent contractors to avoid paying them minimum wage and providing benefits,” according to her campaign website. She also spoke against companies who are increasingly using automation “to evade regulations and eliminate jobs.”
Tech leaders may view a city attorney with an appetite for regulation as “existential to their business model,” said Brian Justie, a researcher at the UCLA Labor Center who was part of the coalition that pushed for the bills.
“What happens in California sets a precedent and serves as a blueprint for the rest of the country,” Justie said. “And so if you’re a Big Tech, you really need to have a certain outcome come to pass here to avoid ripple effects elsewhere.”
For his part, McKinney has blasted Roy for her desire to “turn the city attorney’s office into the country’s largest public interest law firm” as out of touch with what LA voters want. However, voters across the U.S. have increasingly expressed opposition to the expansion of artificial intelligence and the construction of data centers. Roy’s campaign has shown a willingness to lend an ear to growing AI anxieties.
“Billionaires don’t want to answer to the working people, consumers, and communities they exploit,” Roy said in a statement to The Intercept. “But as Los Angeles’ City Attorney, I intend to hold them, their corporations, and the MAGA Republicans that permit their behavior accountable — that’s why they’re spending on someone who won’t.”
McKinney did not respond to The Intercept’s request for comment.
Ads put out by Neighbors for John McKinney assert that McKinney would “take on crooked landlords.” The committee’s website said he would fight for tenant’s “legal protections” against things like “illegal eviction.” But among the committee’s biggest funders is the Santa Monica-based real estate firm, Douglas Emmett Properties, which attempted to carry out one of the largest mass evictions in LA history until it was overruled by a judge. Douglas Emmett donated $250,000 to Neighbors for John McKinney in late September.
Neighbors for John McKinney has also funded attack ads against Roy that paint her as an inexperienced attorney who is weak on crime and has “extreme DSA” positions. The ads cite an article by the conservative California Post, a West Coast spinoff of the New York tabloid, that claimed she had supported a freeze on prosecuting misdemeanors, which she denies.
McKinney campaigns in the mold of law-and-order candidates, pledging to address homelessness and public safety by prosecuting misdemeanors, touting closer relationships with police, and promising to revive a neighborhood prosecutor program. Other California tech-supported efforts have echoed the same — like when tech leaders in the San Francisco Bay Area fueled a successful effort to oust progressive District Attorney Chesa Boudin.
But the LA city attorney’s office holds limited criminal enforcement power, Bonin pointed out. He suspects the tech investment in the LA race is more concerned with potential civil litigation, and he thinks that if voters make that connection, it could spell an issue for the campaign.
“Voters are concerned about Big Tech, they’re certainly concerned about AI, they’re concerned about the influence of — I don’t think you can describe it any other way — 21st-century robber barons,” said Bonin, who now runs the Pat Brown Institute for Public Affairs at California State University, Los Angeles. “Income inequality is a big issue in Los Angeles, so if they make the connection that this funding is symbolic of the agenda that McKinney will pursue … then it becomes more of an issue.”
Roxana Tynan, executive director of the Los Angeles Alliance for a New Economy, called the amount of Big Tech money being spent in the race “outrageous.” As she and other labor rights groups gear up for a fight for more worker AI protections in LA — like expanding safeguards to include temporary and gig workers, and banning employers from using AI software to collect sensitive worker information — she said she hoped people would follow the money being poured into the race and the influence that a few figures look to exert on the city.
“These are people who really believe that not only can they buy elections,” Tynan said, “but that they deserve to buy elections.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

### Key Points

Because California often serves as a legislative blueprint for the rest of the country, tech leaders view the outcome as a critical defense against future labor and AI regulations.
