articles.title: HomePod 27.2 hands-on: default wireless speaker for Mac, Sound Glow and more [Video]
articles.author: Jeff Benjamin
articles.content:
iOS 27.2 and its corresponding updates for the HomePod lineup bring several key new features to Apple’s smart speakers. The most exciting update? The ability to finally use your HomePod as the default sound output for your Mac. This means that the 2nd-generation HomePod and HomePod mini 2 can now function as low-latency wireless speakers for your Mac!
Watch our hands-on video for an in-depth look at how the new wireless speaker functionality works, along with other new features like Sound Glow, Lock Controls, and home theater surround sound support. Be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more in-depth videos.
HomePod as speakers for Mac
It’s long been possible to use a HomePod as a wireless speaker for the Mac, but doing so came with at least one big caveat: wireless latency. While it’s generally fine for movie playback, the latency is immediately noticeable when playing anything in real time. For example, playing instruments in Logic Pro, audio and FaceTime calls, etc. For these particular applications, HomePods have, up until now, been less than ideal speakers for the Mac.
Video walkthrough
Apple has addressed this issue in the 27.2 update, significantly reducing latency when using a HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) as a wireless speaker for Mac desktops and laptops that support Wi-Fi 6E. This, unfortunately, excludes some early Apple Silicon machines, such as those powered by the M1 family of chips, but it’s good to see this feature made available.
For the HomePod mini 2, Apple included a different Wi-Fi/Bluetooth architecture based on PCIe and revised audio routing to prioritize low-latency applications. It’s also worth noting that Apple’s Wi-Fi 6E requirement applies to the Mac hardware itself and doesn’t imply that a user needs a 6E-enabled router.
From that, we can gather that the update will allow the HomePod to work similarly to how it currently works with an Apple TV, when set as the default audio source. In other words, instead of relying on traditional AirPlay, it creates an ad hoc point-to-point connection between the Mac and the HomePod for minimal latency. This will make a HomePod a viable speaker-output destination for real-time audio applications.
Apple is so confident of the low-latency connection that it defaults to playing sound effects via AirPlay when a compatible HomePod is selected as the output destination. Obviously, sound effects are the sort of thing that relies on low latency, since their sound has to correspond to what is happening in the environment at that exact time; otherwise, it would be disorienting. If I select my HomePod mini (1st generation), that option is not even available.
Needless to say, this update instantly has me reconsidering my speaker needs for my Mac desktop setup. I recently got rid of my Yamaha HS3s because I’m looking for something with a little more umph. A pair of full-sized 2nd-generation HomePods in a stereo pair would definitely fit the bill, and look much better to boot.
Lock Controls
Have you ever accidentally brushed the touch sensor on the top cap of the HomePod, activating it to play music? Do you have pets who surreptitiously activate your HomePod while you’re not in the room? If so, then the new Lock Controls switch in 27.2 will help.
When Lock Controls is enabled, the touch surface on top of the HomePod is locked, meaning touch, touch-and-hold, and volume adjustments are disabled. You’ll easily recognize when Lock Controls is enabled by the bright red “no” animation that appears.
Lock Controls will prevent a HomePod from playing audio or taking action when the device’s top cap is touched. However, intercom, alarms, timers, Check in, and FaceTime calls will continue to respond to touch.
Of all the new features in the 27.2 software update, Lock Controls is the only one that appears on all HomePod models, regardless of generation. That means that, yes, even the original OG HomePod lands support for the handy new addition!
Sound Glow
My favorite new feature in the 27.2 update is Sound Glow. This is the feature that displays ambient light that corresponds to the colors and rhythm of the album artwork for the music or podcasts being played.
Sound Glow takes full advantage of the LED Matrix displays beneath the HomePod top cap. The big HomePod features an array of 37 RGB LEDs, while the smaller HomePod mini features an array of 19 RGB LEDs. As a side note, the original HomePod features 19 LEDs across a smaller surface area than the updated version.
To enable Sound Glow, you must update your iOS device and your HomePod to 27.2. Once updated, open the Home app and venture into the settings for the HomePod you wish to adjust. There, you’ll find a Sound Glow switch you can enable.
Apple notes that you’ll also be able to toggle Sound Glow with your voice, but it will require an Apple Intelligence‑enabled iPhone running the latest software. This could be enabled once Apple enables Siri AI on the HomePod mini 2, and perhaps the 2nd-generation HomePod, but this remains to be seen.
Home theater surround sound
If you plan to purchase an Apple TV 4K (fourth-generation), you’re likely interested in the new home theater surround sound option available with the HomePod mini 2 or the 2nd-generation full-sized HomePod. This feature lets you use four HomePods, two identical matching stereo pairs in front and rear, for a surround sound setup.
I haven’t been able to personally test this yet, because I don’t yet have the newest Apple TV 4K, but I can bet it will sound fantastic, especially when four full-sized Dolby Atmos-enabled HomePods are involved. That being said, this is an expensive proposition.
Here are the pricing details for those looking to set up a four-speaker home theater surround sound option:
- Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod 2 ($349×4) = $1695
- Apple TV 4K ($299) + Two HomePod 2 ($349×2) + two HomePod mini 2 ($149×2) = $1295
- Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod mini 2 ($149×4) = $895
By way of comparison, Sonos’ Dolby Atmos-enabled four-speaker Immersive Set with Beam Ultra bundle can be had for less than $1600 and comes with a dedicated subwoofer. I’m not a home audio expert or an audiophile, so I can’t say which one is better, but it’s interesting that both it and the highest-tier HomePod surround setup are so similar in price.
When managing your HomePod speakers via the tvOS interface on the Apple TV 4K, you’ll see new options for Surround Sound and Whole Room Audio under the Home Theater section. The surround sound option is self-explanatory and ideal for movies and television shows, but the Whole Room Audio option is better suited to listening to music, as it provides left- and right-channel placement no matter which direction you face.
9to5Mac’s Take
iOS 27.2 provides noteworthy updates to all HomePod models, including the original HomePod, which now includes the new Lock Controls capability. But the real fun starts with the HomePod mini, with its Sound Glow support, and the HomePod mini 2 and HomePod 2nd-generation, with their support for working as the default speaker for Wi-Fi 6E-enabled Mac hardware. I think a pair of HomePod mini 2’s would look great sitting next to Apple’s just-released M6 iMac.
What do you think? Are you planning to get any of Apple’s new Home-focused hardware, or are you looking to take advantage of the new 27.2 features on hardware you already own? Sound off in the comments with your thoughts on the matter.
articles.summary:
Apple’s 27.2 software update introduces low-latency Mac audio support, new Lock Controls for all models, and immersive surround sound configurations for the latest HomePod and HomePod mini devices.

### Key Points
- HomePod (2nd generation) and HomePod mini 2 now support low-latency wireless audio for Macs equipped with Wi-Fi 6E.
- The new Lock Controls feature disables touch-surface inputs on all HomePod generations to prevent accidental activation by users or pets.
- Sound Glow provides ambient LED lighting that syncs with the rhythm and colors of album artwork on supported HomePod models.
- Users can now configure four-speaker surround sound setups when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
- The update enables an ad hoc point-to-point connection, allowing HomePods to function as viable speakers for real-time audio applications like Logic Pro.

### Why it Matters
These updates transform the HomePod lineup from simple smart speakers into more versatile components for professional desktop setups and home theater environments. By reducing latency and expanding configuration options, Apple is positioning its hardware as a more competitive alternative to dedicated third-party audio systems.

articles.title: Lord Of The Rings RPG Game Studio Hit By ‘Serious’ Cyberattack As The Internet Continues Breaking
articles.author: Ethan Gach
articles.content:
Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 maker Warhorse Studios is the latest video game company to get hit with a cyberattack. The company, which is working on an open-world RPG adaptation of The Lord of the Rings, said it’s still assessing the damage from the security breach.
“Warhorse Studios confirms that it has been the target of a cyberattack,” the studio wrote in an announcement on its website. “We are working with cybersecurity experts to secure our systems, investigate the incident, and assess its full impact. The attack involved unauthorized access to company systems as well as access to company data. We are coordinating with the relevant authorities as the investigation continues.”
“This is a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and everyone affected,” CEO Martin Frývaldský said. “Our immediate priority is to secure our systems, establish the full extent of the breach, and take the necessary steps to protect our employees, partners, and community. We are dedicating the resources needed to address this situation and will communicate further information as soon as we responsibly can.”
It’s unclear what data, if any, was stolen. Anyone operating online, including gaming companies, has recently been threatened by a rash of security vulnerabilities surfaced by AI. Bad actors can also use AI to take advantage of exploits that otherwise wouldn’t be feasible to attempt manually. An issue with PHP, a scripting language upon which much of the modern web is built, led a number of websites to go offline recently. Some older browser games have had to discontinue service entirely.
“To further strengthen security related to the PHP programming language used in the PlayStation 4 and Steam versions of Street Fighter V, content requiring online functionality is currently unavailable,” Capcom announced overnight. “Offline content remains available and can still be enjoyed. Emergency maintenance is currently underway to address this issue. Until the fix has been completed, sales on the PlayStation Store and Steam will be suspended in stages. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience this has caused and appreciate your patience and understanding.”
Capcom and Square Enix have also recently suffered online breaches, though the two gaming companies didn’t specify whether the recent cyberattacks were likely powered by AI or not.
articles.summary:
Warhorse Studios, the developer behind Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, has confirmed a significant cyberattack involving unauthorized access to company systems and internal data currently under investigation by experts.

### Key Points
- Warhorse Studios is working with cybersecurity professionals and authorities to assess the full extent of the data breach.
- CEO Martin Frývaldský stated that the company is prioritizing system security and the protection of employees, partners, and the community.
- The incident follows a recent trend of cyberattacks affecting major gaming companies, including recent security issues at Capcom and Square Enix.
- Capcom recently suspended online functionality and sales for Street Fighter V on Steam and PlayStation to address vulnerabilities related to the PHP scripting language.

### Why it Matters
The gaming industry is facing an increasing frequency of cyberattacks, potentially exacerbated by new AI-driven exploitation methods. These security breaches threaten sensitive corporate data and disrupt online services, forcing developers to prioritize infrastructure stability over ongoing operations.

articles.title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted For Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm. According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top. The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica's 2019 article "The Trade Secret," which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme.
The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets' files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi's Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms. "By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself," U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. "Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity." [...] Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any particular method. "How we do it, it's our problem," he told ProPublica. "You will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride." He called MonsterCloud's data recovery methods a "trade secret."
[...] Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about $8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison. [...] In 2019, Pinhasi touted MonsterCloud's ties to law enforcement as evidence of its integrity. Pistole, who also headed the Transportation Security Administration under President Barack Obama, was listed on MonsterCloud's website as the only member of its "Cyber Security Advisory Council."
articles.summary:
Florida-based data recovery firm owner Zohar Pinhasi faces federal fraud charges for allegedly paying hackers to unlock client files while falsely claiming to use proprietary decryption methods.

### Key Points
- Zohar Pinhasi, operating under the alias Zack Green, allegedly defrauded clients of his company, MonsterCloud, by secretly paying ransoms he claimed to bypass.
- Federal investigators report that Pinhasi collected over $19 million from victims while paying out approximately $8 million in ransom demands.
- One documented case involved Pinhasi charging a client $150,000 for a recovery process that cost him only $8,200 in ransom payments.
- The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation that exposed the firm's deceptive business practices and misleading claims regarding its recovery methods.
- Pinhasi faces a potential sentence of up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted of the charges.

### Why it Matters
This case highlights the significant risks businesses face when hiring third-party firms to manage ransomware incidents without verifying their recovery protocols. It serves as a warning to organizations that deceptive intermediaries can exploit security crises to extract excessive fees, further victimizing those already targeted by cybercriminals.

articles.title: As Anthropic’s IPO approaches, CFO Krishna Rao faces a defining test
articles.author: Sheryl Estrada
articles.content:
Good morning. Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao faces a defining question as the AI company prepares to go public: Can extraordinary revenue growth translate into sustainable profitability as the cost of advanced AI systems mount?
Anthropic filed its Form S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday for a proposed Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. Revenue reached $16.29 billion for the six months ended June 30, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier. Net loss totaled $80.75 billion, largely reflecting a $72.39 billion accounting charge tied to changes in the fair value of financing instruments, Fortune reported. Operating loss narrowed to $693 million from $2.14 billion.
Founded in 2021 and led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic develops the Claude family of AI models and products, including Claude Code and Claude Cowork. In May, the company raised $65 billion in a funding round that valued it at $965 billion post-money.
Growth raises infrastructure stakes
Anthropic’s enterprise business is expanding rapidly. As of Sept. 30, more than 11,900 customers generated at least $100,000 in revenue for the company over the trailing 12 months, including approximately 250 that generated at least $10 million.
For Rao, Anthropic’s first CFO, appointed in 2024, financing that growth means securing the computing capacity needed to sustain it without allowing infrastructure commitments to overwhelm the business.
On the Invest Like the Best podcast in May, Rao said he devotes 30% to 40% of his time to compute infrastructure.
“The compute that we procure is the lifeblood of our business,” he said. Anthropic uses Amazon’s Trainium chips, Google’s tensor processing units and Nvidia’s graphics processing units.
Compute and infrastructure expenses reached $8.95 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $2.33 billion a year earlier. Anthropic says it currently makes more than two dollars in revenue for every dollar it spends on computing infrastructure; but that could change if the AI lab is forced to reduce token prices, a risk it warns about in its S-1 filing, Fortune reported.
Although revenue growth has outpaced the increase in this major cost category, that alone doesn’t establish improving unit economics or a clear path to profitability. Other expenses, contractual commitments and future capacity needs will also shape returns.
Investors weigh returns and risks
Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told me the filing is “a watershed event for the tech sector and AI Revolution.” Analysts at the firm highlighted compute constraints, limited shareholder influence and potential conflicts between Anthropic’s public-benefit mandate and financial returns.
“The near term losses are massive, but investors on the IPO will be laser focused on the growth trajectory into 2027 and 2028,” the analysts wrote in a note.
Raj Joshi, senior vice president of Moody’s Ratings Corporate Finance Group, told me in an email that the filing would “shine a brighter light on the AI labs’ finances, as well as contracts with Big Tech companies, enhancing investors’ ability to assess risk across the sector.”
Anthropic also warns that falling behind competitors in developing advanced AI models could weaken demand even as infrastructure costs remain substantial.
For Rao, the test is whether Anthropic can sustain its extraordinary growth while improving operating performance and managing its computing commitments. Investors must weigh that opportunity against competitive pressures and governance risks.

Average support for shareholder proposals rose to 27.9% from 24.3% in 2025, even as the number of environmental and social proposals voted on fell 47%; proposals seeking political-spending disclosures attracted record average support of 42%. Director support remained high, while say-on-pay approval reached a 10-year high of 88.9%.
Retail investors owned 6 billion more shares and voted 2 billion more shares than the previous season, alongside broader adoption of pass-through voting and virtual shareholder meetings. Together, these trends point to sustained support for corporate leadership, more selective shareholder-proposal activity, and an expanding range of tools for shareholder engagement.
Going deeper
Microsoft is offering buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees, or about 27% of its workforce, as the software giant continues to spend heavily on AI, Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera reports. Chief people officer Amy Coleman introduced the new program on Monday, noting that eligible employees include senior leaders, up to vice presidents. Read more here.
Overheard
“AI will commoditize plenty of tasks, but it will not commoditize the people who know which tasks matter.”
—Jay Kaplan, co-founder and CEO of Synack, writes in a Fortune opinion piece. Synack completed its merger with NetSPI in October. Before founding Synack in 2013, Kaplan worked in computer network operations at the National Security Agency.
articles.summary:
AI developer Anthropic has filed for a Nasdaq initial public offering under the ticker ANT, reporting significant revenue growth alongside substantial infrastructure costs and net losses.

### Key Points
- Anthropic reported $16.29 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026, a sharp increase from $1.16 billion during the same period last year.
- The company recorded a net loss of $80.75 billion, largely driven by an accounting charge related to the fair value of financing instruments.
- Infrastructure and compute expenses reached $8.95 billion in the first half of 2026 as the firm scales its Claude AI model family.
- As of September 30, the company served over 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue.
- Anthropic currently maintains a valuation of $965 billion following a $65 billion funding round completed in May.

### Why it Matters
This IPO serves as a critical test for the AI sector, highlighting the tension between rapid revenue scaling and the massive capital requirements of high-performance computing. Investors will closely monitor whether Anthropic can achieve sustainable profitability while managing intense competitive pressures and significant infrastructure commitments.

articles.title: Russia jails IT worker for 13 years for donating money to Ukraine
articles.author: Heba Habib
articles.content:
A Russian military court has sentenced an IT specialist to 13 years in prison for financing “terrorism” after the cryptocurrency exchange Binance gave Russian investigators details of his donations to Ukrainian fundraising campaigns.
The 2nd Western District Military Court on Monday convicted 49-year-old Yuri Belenkiy and sentenced him to three years in prison followed by 10 years in a strict-regime penal colony, according to a court statement.
Russian state news agency TASS reported that Belenkiy is a former IT director of the company DiHouse and that prosecutors had asked for 14 years. He was also fined 500,000 roubles ($6,300).
Belenkiy, who holds a Bulgarian residence permit, was detained in September last year when he flew to Moscow for a visit. He denied the charges, and his defence will appeal the verdict, according to TASS.
According to the RIA Novosti news agency, the court found that between August 2022 and March 2024, Belenkiy made 15 cryptocurrency transfers worth more than 120,000 roubles ($1,500) to fund Ukraine’s armed forces and the Azov battalion, which Russia designates a “terrorist” organisation. He used payment details posted by Arkady Babchenko, an exiled Russian journalist and Kremlin critic. RIA added that Belenkiy is on the Russian financial monitoring agency’s list of “terrorists and extremists”.
Russian law enforcement documents seen by the Reuters news agency showed that Binance gave investigators Belenkiy’s transaction history in response to a Russian request. The documents also showed that the records were instrumental in prosecuting him.
“The response from Binance serves as key evidence in the criminal case against Belenkiy,” Yevgeny Smirnov, a lawyer with the rights group First Department, which assists people facing politically motivated prosecutions in Russia, told Reuters.
In court, however, the defence questioned whether the data really came from Binance, noting that the exchange has not cooperated with Russia since 2022, TASS reported.
Asked about the sentence, Binance referred Reuters to a previous statement saying the exchange “does not make or enforce the laws of any jurisdiction, determine charges, or decide how any government uses information in legal proceedings”. It said it does not comment on confidential law enforcement requests or individual cases.
Binance pulled out of the Russian market in 2023, after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Western sanctions that followed. Mike Bystrov, a lawyer specialising in crypto regulation, told Reuters in August that the exchange had been under no obligation to provide Belenkiy’s data. Because of Belenkiy’s Bulgarian residency, Bystrov said, Binance may in fact have been obliged under European Union data protection law not to do so.
First Department claimed in a recent report that about 10 percent of all charges brought under the country’s treason and espionage laws in 2025 were linked to donations to Ukrainian organisations. The group said authorities track cryptocurrency transfers as well as bank payments, and continue to open cases over donations made as early as 2022.
articles.summary:
A Russian military court sentenced IT specialist Yuri Belenkiy to 13 years in prison for financing terrorism after Binance provided his cryptocurrency transaction history to Russian investigators.

### Key Points
- Yuri Belenkiy, a 49-year-old former IT director, received a 13-year sentence for donating over 120,000 roubles to Ukrainian military causes.
- The 2nd Western District Military Court convicted Belenkiy for transfers made between August 2022 and March 2024 to groups including the Azov battalion.
- Court documents reveal that Binance provided the defendant's transaction history to Russian authorities, which served as primary evidence in the criminal case.
- Belenkiy, who holds a Bulgarian residence permit, was arrested in September 2023 upon arriving in Moscow and plans to appeal the verdict.
- The Russian financial monitoring agency currently lists Belenkiy as a terrorist and extremist, and he was fined 500,000 roubles.

### Why it Matters
This case highlights the significant risks associated with using centralized cryptocurrency exchanges that may comply with international law enforcement requests. It also underscores how Russian authorities are increasingly utilizing digital financial records to prosecute citizens for supporting Ukrainian organizations, even when those individuals reside abroad.

articles.title: NY Gov. Hochul once resisted a data center pause. Now it’s central to her campaign.
articles.author: Jon Campbell
articles.content:
Six months ago, when a group of New York lawmakers began pushing for a moratorium on large-scale data centers, Gov. Kathy Hochul was unconvinced.
In May, the governor told reporters she wanted to take steps to ensure local communities benefit if they allow a data center in their backyard. But she said an outright pause wasn’t on the table.
“I'm not talking about a flat-out moratorium,” Hochul said at the time, adding that she doesn’t want to be “inhospitable” to a growing industry.
Just two months later, in July, the governor reversed course, announcing her own year-long moratorium on large-scale data centers. She has since made it a centerpiece of her reelection campaign.
Hochul said the pause – the first such data center moratorium in the country – would allow the state to craft a regulatory scheme.
Hochul said New York has 30 pending applications under consideration and the scale of the projects helped convince her it was important to “step back and let the state take control,” as she told ABC News. “New York doesn't just want to be first. We want to be the first to get it right.”
Hochul has put the moratorium, and bringing down costs for average New Yorkers, at the center of her closing pitch to New York voters ahead of Election Day, highlighting it in advertisements and using it to paint a clear line of demarcation between herself and her Republican opponent, Bruce Blakeman, who opposes the pause.
Hochul’s evolution tracks with the public’s souring on data centers, which use large amounts of water and electricity and have become especially unpopular across much of the country.
But Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, has accused Hochul of creating “a hostile atmosphere to businesses.”
Blakeman says the moratorium could stifle innovation in artificial intelligence – and end up costing New Yorkers. And while he acknowledges there are issues with data centers that have to be addressed, including water and energy supply, he faults Hochul for “saying no to the fastest-growing industry in the world.”
“ You put a ban in because you said that you needed time to figure it out,” Blakeman said during the debate. “What have you been doing for the last four years?”
Public polling suggests Hochul’s change of heart may be good politics.
A Siena University poll in August found voters supported her moratorium by a 2-to-1 margin, not long after Hochul put it in place.
The next month, 63% of voters said they wouldn’t want a data center near their area of the state after the moratorium expires, according to Siena.
But at the same time, few voters rank data centers as their top priority in the race. Just 2% of likely voters said AI data centers are the most important thing on their mind when choosing whether to vote for Hochul and Blakeman, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released last week. That’s compared to 22% who said the economy and 19% who said cost of living — two issues that arguably overlap with data centers.
At least 15 other states are considering a ban or moratorium of their own, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Hochul’s moratorium, meanwhile, seeks to walk a fine line between satisfying the concerns of everyday New Yorkers without turning off the tech giants looking to build the facilities in the Empire State.
So far, it seems to be working. Julie Samuels, president and CEO of Tech:NYC, said the major tech trade group supports Hochul’s approach over a bill the state Legislature ultimately approved in June, which goes further than Hochul’s moratorium.
“The governor in this case took what I think is a pretty moderate position in trying to find a path forward,” said Samuels, whose group includes major players in the AI industry, including Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI.
The governor’s pause, laid out in an executive order, applies to larger data centers that can consume at least 50 megawatts of energy, which is enough to power upwards of 45,000 homes. It is meant to give the state time to craft a wide-ranging “environmental impact statement” that will assess a variety of issues associated with data centers, including energy demand, water use and noise levels.
The Legislature’s moratorium, by contrast, would apply to projects that consume at least 20 megawatts of power, including smaller or regional facilities. It would also require data centers to produce their own energy, with a certain percentage required to be renewable – a provision that isn’t in Hochul’s order.
Hochul has until the end of the year to sign or veto the Legislature’s bill, and she has yet to take a position. But Hochul said that whatever she does, she will ensure data facilities must “bring their own power” or pay a premium for electricity.
She also wants a policy in place that ensures that the local community gets “millions of dollars” worth of benefits, such as an investment fund that pays for infrastructure upgrades. The Hochul administration suggests local governments should get $1 million in benefits for each megawatt a data center demands, meaning a 50 megawatt facility should result in a $50 million benefit.
“ I'm trying to have a smart policy,” she said during the debate. “We are pro-technology, pro-innovation.”
Blakeman, meanwhile, said Hochul’s policy was too little, too late and has harmed the state’s standing with businesses looking to come to New York.
“Why didn’t you get all the stakeholders in the same room and figure it out, instead of saying no to the fastest-growing industry in the world?” he asked Hochul during the debate.
articles.summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has implemented a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers to establish new environmental regulations, marking a significant shift in her administration's technology policy.

### Key Points
- The executive order pauses new data center projects consuming 50 megawatts or more of energy, enough to power approximately 45,000 homes.
- Governor Hochul intends to use the year-long window to develop an environmental impact statement addressing water usage, noise levels, and energy demand.
- The administration proposes that future data centers provide $1 million in local community benefits for every megawatt of power consumed.
- Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman criticizes the move as anti-business, arguing it stifles artificial intelligence innovation and creates a hostile environment for technology companies.
- A Siena University poll indicates that New York voters support the moratorium by a 2-to-1 margin, despite few ranking the issue as a top priority.
- At least 15 other states are currently considering similar legislative bans or moratoriums on large-scale data center development.

### Why it Matters
This policy shift highlights the growing tension between the massive energy requirements of the artificial intelligence industry and the infrastructure concerns of local communities. By balancing regulatory oversight with economic development, the state's approach could serve as a national model for how governments manage the rapid expansion of high-demand digital infrastructure.

articles.title: Satechi’s Dual-Monitor Adapter Gives Its USB-C Plug a Parking Spot
articles.author: JC Torres
articles.content:
Laptops may have become easier to carry, but the desk you return to can still demand a handful of connections. Satechi’s new ExtendView USB4 Dual HDMI Multiport Adapter gathers two monitors and other accessories behind one laptop cable. It’s a familiar idea with a welcome physical detail: the attached connector has somewhere to go when it’s time to pack the adapter away.
Rather than hide under the desk, the Space Black anodized aluminum enclosure has enough character to sit beside a laptop. Rounded corners soften its rectangular shape, while a regular pattern of small dots gives the top some texture. The connections occupy opposite long edges, separating the monitor and power cables from the USB accessories you might reach for more often during work.
Designer: Satechi
The more interesting detail, however, appears when you’re putting it away. The braided nylon cable loops back so its USB-C connector can tuck into a slot in the body. That doesn’t make the cable disappear, of course, but it keeps the plug from dangling freely inside your bag. That’s a small convenience, but a welcome one if you’re constantly changing where you work.
Back at the desk, two HDMI ports support separate extended displays at up to 4K and 60Hz each. Your editing timeline can occupy one screen while reference material stays open on the other, rather than both repeating the same picture. Satechi says compatible computers need no DisplayLink software or additional drivers, using the display capabilities already available through their own USB4 connections.
That compatibility comes with qualifications worth reading before buying. Base M3 MacBooks need their lids closed to run two external displays, while base M1 and M2 Mac laptops remain limited to one. A USB-C socket alone doesn’t guarantee the right capabilities, either. The two-monitor arrangement needs a suitable USB4 connection and a computer that can actually support both screens through that connection.
There’s room for the smaller things that accumulate around those larger screens, too. Two USB-A ports and two USB-C data ports support speeds up to 10Gbps, accommodating an external drive alongside other accessories. Those USB-C ports don’t output video, despite looking like the laptop connection. Keeping a project drive within reach makes sense, particularly when the monitor cables can stay on the opposite side.
Charging deserves a closer look, however, because the advertised 140W figure refers to incoming power. Satechi’s technical documentation specifies up to 125W for the laptop, reserving about 15W for the adapter itself. You’ll need an appropriate charger and cable to reach its maximum, with actual delivery also depending on your laptop. Convenient pass-through charging, certainly, but the distinction matters before buying a power supply.
At $119.99, the ExtendView is listed on Satechi’s US store as a compact alternative to a larger desktop dock. Its attached cable does introduce a tradeoff: a damaged lead can’t simply be unplugged and replaced. Giving that connector a storage slot is welcome, then, even if it can’t offer the flexibility of a cable you can swap out yourself at home.
articles.summary:
Satechi has launched the ExtendView USB4 Dual HDMI Multiport Adapter, a compact docking solution designed to support dual 4K displays and multiple peripherals through a single laptop connection.

### Key Points
- The adapter features two HDMI ports supporting 4K resolution at 60Hz for extended display setups.
- It includes two USB-A and two USB-C data ports capable of transfer speeds up to 10Gbps.
- The device supports up to 125W of pass-through charging for laptops when paired with a 140W power supply.
- A built-in storage slot for the integrated braided nylon cable prevents the connector from dangling during transport.
- Compatibility varies by model, with base M1 and M2 MacBooks limited to a single external display.
- The unit is currently available on the Satechi US store for $119.99.

### Why it Matters
This adapter offers a portable alternative to bulky desktop docks for professionals who frequently transition between mobile and stationary workspaces. By streamlining cable management and display connectivity, it simplifies hardware integration for users with limited desk space or high-performance peripheral needs.

articles.title: Apple Fixes Possibly Exploited CoreGraphics Flaw on Older iPhones
articles.author: Tim Hardwick
articles.content:
Among the flurry of iOS 27.2 releases on Monday, Apple also pushed a wave of software updates for its older operating systems, including a fix for a CoreGraphics vulnerability that Apple says may have been exploited in targeted attacks.
The releases include iOS 26.7.2, iPadOS 26.7.2, iOS 18.7.11, iPadOS 18.7.11, macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, macOS Sequoia 15.8.2, and tvOS 26.6.1.
iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 bring the CoreGraphics fix to the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad, all of which cannot run iOS 26. According to Apple, processing a maliciously crafted file on these devices could lead to arbitrary code execution, and the company is "aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27."
For iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2, Apple lists security fixes covering 134 vulnerabilities, none of which are flagged as having been exploited in the wild.
Apple likewise lists security fixes for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.2.
Lastly, tvOS 26.6.1: the only release of these updates with a user-facing change. The update adds support for the fourth-generation Siri Remote on the Apple TV HD and first-generation Apple TV 4K.
All of the updates are available now. On iPhone and iPad, go to Settings ➝ General ➝ Software Update. On Mac, go to System Settings ➝ General ➝ Software Update. On Apple TV, open up Settings and go to System ➝ Software Update.
articles.summary:
Apple has released a series of critical software updates across its ecosystem to address a CoreGraphics vulnerability that may have been exploited in targeted attacks against users.

### Key Points
- Apple issued security patches for iOS 26.7.2, iPadOS 26.7.2, iOS 18.7.11, iPadOS 18.7.11, macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, macOS Sequoia 15.8.2, and tvOS 26.6.1.
- The CoreGraphics vulnerability in iOS 18.7.11 allows for arbitrary code execution and affects older devices like the iPhone XS, XR, and seventh-generation iPad.
- Apple confirmed reports that the CoreGraphics flaw was utilized in sophisticated, targeted attacks prior to the release of iOS 27.
- The iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2 updates include patches for 134 distinct security vulnerabilities.
- The tvOS 26.6.1 update introduces support for the fourth-generation Siri Remote on Apple TV HD and first-generation Apple TV 4K models.

### Why it Matters
These updates are essential for protecting users against active security threats that could allow unauthorized code execution on older hardware. Promptly installing these patches ensures that devices remain secure against known exploits while maintaining compatibility with newer peripheral hardware.
